newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lebanese denies starting fatal German hostel fire.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese denies starting fatal German hostel fire.

text.p: A young Lebanese refugee on trial in Germany for starting a fire that killed 10 people in an asylum-seekers' hostel last January told the court on Wednesday he was asleep when the fire broke out.
Safwan Eid, a civil war refugee who had lived in the hostel in the northern city of Luebeck since 1990 with nine members of his family, described how he was woken by cries for help.

Eid said he and his brother who shared a bedroom could not get out of the burning building. "It was impossible to escape by the stairway which was filled with smoke. The only way out was on to the roof," he said.
He and his brother were then rescued by firemen, Eid told the court in a mixture of broken German and Arabic.

Eid is charged with aggravated arson and negligently causing bodily harm for allegedly starting the fire that killed six Zaireans, a man from Benin, a Lebanese and an Angolan woman with her six-year-old daughter. Thirty-eight people were injured.

The blaze was the worst disaster ever to hit an asylum-seekers' home in Germany and recalled an upsurge of neo-Nazi violence, including firebomb attacks on Turkish homes in Solingen and Moelln, following German unification in 1990.
Prosecutors say Eid started the fire in a petty act of vengeance on a neighbour, and base their case on three words Eid allegedly told a first aider after he was rescued: "It was us."
Eid, however, told the court that what he really said was: "It was them -- they set the stairs on fire," repeating something his father had just told him.
Asked by one of his defence team what his father had meant, Safwan Eid said: "It was obvious that when he said they' he was talking about the Nazis."
Anti-racist and left-wing groups say the fire was a neo-Nazi attack and the accused was a victim.
Eid's defence team argue that prosecutors did not properly investigate four youths, including a skinhead from a local far-right group, who were detained near the scene.
Three of the young men, driving a stolen car, had singed hair. But police accepted their alibis and released them.
Eid could face life imprisonment if convicted, unless the court decides to treat him as a juvenile.

Eid gave his age as 20, which means he could be treated as a juvenile at the court's discretion and be liable for a maximum 10-year sentence. But prosecutors say he was already 21 at the time of the fire and must therefore face an adult penalty.
